Supervision note, 18 July. Written by Bhupen, partnerships manager.

I explained that Mr. Tanaka, like several of our partners there, tends to say no politely: "a little difficult" and a long silence usually mean no. A blunt yes-or-no question can put him on the spot.
Since then I have watched her adapt. On this week's call she asked, "What date would feel comfortable for your team?" and listened to the pauses. She also checked with Ms. Mori, their coordinator, afterwards. The date she got was realistic.
Next step: I will ask Ishita to share this with the two new joiners.

qa.a: On the 14th of the next month.

qa.a: Ishita felt hopeful and took it as a maybe, then was likely frustrated and embarrassed when the parts came weeks late.

qa.q: How did Ishita adapt her questions?
qa.a: She asked open questions like what date would feel comfortable, listened to the pauses, and checked with the coordinator, Ms. Mori, afterwards.

qa.q: How might Mr. Tanaka have felt being asked 'yes or no?'
qa.a: He may have felt put on the spot and uncomfortable, preferring to decline politely rather than say a blunt no.

grounding: A supervisor notes a young professional learning that a softener and silence meant no, and adapting to a partner's indirect style.

Tuesday night
Asked Vinita-di today, straight out, "Will you write me a reference for the Pune job?" In my family we just ask. But she looked at her tea for ages and said, "Hmm. Let's see. These weeks are very busy, na..." and then changed the subject to the canteen samosas.
At first I thought that meant yes, later. Then I remembered how Mamta-di explained things when I joined: with some seniors here, "let's see" plus a long silence is a polite no. Nobody says no to your face.
Stung a bit, honestly. But she didn't want to embarrass me, and maybe she doesn't know my work well enough.
So I won't push. Tomorrow I'll ask Mamta-di, who does know my work, whether she'd feel comfortable writing it. And I'll ask in a way that makes no easy to say.
Binita

Suraj had been posted to the village near Dharwad for three weeks when he asked old Basappa directly, outside the tea shop, "Can we use your field for the new seed trial?"
Basappa smiled, looked at the sky and said, "Let's see after the rains." Then he talked about his grandson's cricket for ten minutes.
Suraj wrote "maybe yes" in his notebook.
Pooja, the local health worker, laughed when she saw it. "That was a no, Suraj. A polite one. You asked him in front of six men; he couldn't refuse you straight."
"Then how do I ever know?"
"Watch what comes after. A real maybe asks questions. He changed the subject. Next time, ask quietly, or ask through someone he trusts."
